findings.description: Duplicate verdicts are accepted if a later row supersedes their shared hash. Given two identical rows A followed by B with supersedes=sha256(A), pos collapses both copies of A and the effective-row loop skips both before checking duplicates. The file passes despite the second A lacking the required supersedes reference.
findings.failure_mode: When a verdict file contains duplicated original rows followed by a correction, grading succeeds and reports only one superseded row, violating the documented one-to-one binding and duplicate-rejection contract.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate duplicate pairs and supersession incrementally in file order. Reject every subsequent row unless it explicitly supersedes the current effective row, and reject repeated row hashes before constructing hash-indexed maps.
findings.failure_scenario: When a verdict file contains duplicated original rows followed by a correction, grading succeeds and reports only one superseded row, violating the documented one-to-one binding and duplicate-rejection contract.

findings.description: write_layout() joins each (rel, bytes) entry straight onto the fixture directory: dest = os.path.join(fdir, sub, rel), then os.makedirs(dirname(dest)) and open(dest, 'wb'). There is no containment check on rel. An absolute rel makes os.path.join discard fdir entirely ('/home/x/.bashrc'), and a '..' component or a tree entry literally named '..' walks out of <corpus>/<fx>/head. The library already has exactly the right guard for labels (head_path: refuses absolute paths, backslash, NUL, '..' segments and verifies realpath stays under head/) but the layout writer, which is the function the new seed-corpus-from-external.sh is documented to share for repositories it does not control, does not use it. Reviewer concern 6 asks precisely about path traversal in tree entries reaching the fixture writer; the truncated external seeder is not shown to reject such entries before this call, and the record seeder's paths come from git tree listings that git itself does not guarantee are '..'-free.
findings.failure_mode: When the external seeder passes a hostile repository's tree-entry path such as '../../../../home/runner/.ssh/authorized_keys' or '/etc/cron.d/x' into write_layout, then the seeder creates directories and overwrites that file with attacker-chosen bytes outside the fixture directory, with the invoking user's privileges, before any SHA256SUMS or no-secrets pass runs.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate every rel in write_layout with the same rule as head_path before writing: reject empty, absolute, backslash, NUL, and any '.'/'..' segment; compute dest and assert os.path.realpath(dest).startswith(os.path.realpath(os.path.join(fdir, sub)) + os.sep); fail() on violation. Do this in the library (the sink) so both seeders are covered regardless of caller sanitisation; add a corpus-seed-lib.bats case with rel values '../x', '/x', 'a/../../x' and '..'.
findings.failure_scenario: When the external seeder passes a hostile repository's tree-entry path such as '../../../../home/runner/.ssh/authorized_keys' or '/etc/cron.d/x' into write_layout, then the seeder creates directories and overwrites that file with attacker-chosen bytes outside the fixture directory, with the invoking user's privileges, before any SHA256SUMS or no-secrets pass runs.

findings.description: The 1.5.0 header promises that with --judge-verdicts every row of this run is validated and that a row whose pair this grade does not credit 'is stale and rejects the grade (exit 2, no grade.json written)'. judge_fields() is only reached inside the review-catch branch after grade_recall (line 3445) and, for --union, only inside 'if valid_ids:' (line 3575). A review-catch run that never reaches recall scoring (no review.md, refused, timed-out, sandbox copy failure) or a cell with no valid session therefore writes grade.json with no fixture_sha256 / credited_pairs / judge block and never checks the file's rows for that run_id, even though by construction none of them can be a credited pair.
findings.failure_mode: When an operator re-grades a failed run or an empty union cell with a verdicts file that still carries rows for that run id, then the grader exits 0 and writes a grade.json without the judge fields instead of rejecting the stale rows, so a downstream reads.py --judge-defects pass sees neither the stale rows nor an empty credited_pairs listing and cannot tell 'nothing to judge' from 'judge binding skipped'.
findings.suggested_fix: When JUDGE[0] is set and the review-catch path exits before recall is scored (and in grade_union when valid_ids is empty), still call judge_fields with cites=[] and recall=None so that any row of this run is rejected as stale per the spec and an otherwise empty credited_pairs/judge block is recorded; or raise GradeError explicitly stating the run credits no pairs.
findings.failure_scenario: When an operator re-grades a failed run or an empty union cell with a verdicts file that still carries rows for that run id, then the grader exits 0 and writes a grade.json without the judge fields instead of rejecting the stale rows, so a downstream reads.py --judge-defects pass sees neither the stale rows nor an empty credited_pairs listing and cannot tell 'nothing to judge' from 'judge binding skipped'.

findings.description: On reviewer concern 10 (divergence from lib/jcs.sh changing a supersedes hash): a verdict row's hash cannot diverge between serialisers because every row field is pattern-bound to ASCII with no control characters and there are no numeric fields, so string-escaping and number-formatting differences are unreachable there. The one exposed hash is fixture_sha256 = jcs_sha(t.key) over the key manifest. Within jcs_number the shortcut 'if x.is_integer() and abs(x) < 1e21: return str(int(x))' is not RFC 8785 conformant for integral doubles above 2^53: ECMAScript Number::toString uses the shortest round-trip digits padded with zeros (1.2345678901234568e20 -> '123456789012345680000') while str(int(x)) prints the exact binary value ('123456789012345683968'). The general repr-based path below already handles integral floats correctly (repr(100.0)='100.0' -> '100'), so the shortcut is both unnecessary and wrong. Likewise the int branch str(x) emits all digits for ints >= 1e21 where the RFC requires exponent form. Neither is reachable with today's manifests (anchor lines <= 10M), but the function is presented as an RFC 8785 serialiser and is paired with a separate jq/shell implementation.
findings.failure_mode: When a future key manifest carries a numeric value above 2^53 (or a string with DEL/U+007F, which jq-based serialisers escape as \u007f and Python does not), then ablation-grade.sh and lib/jcs.sh compute different fixture_sha256 values for the same key and every verdict row is rejected as stale with a misleading 'the key changed' message.
findings.suggested_fix: Delete the str(int(x)) shortcut and route all finite floats through the repr-based algorithm; for ints outside +/-2^53 convert through float(x) first (or refuse with GradeError since the key schema never needs them). Add a shared vector test that hashes every manifest under grimoires/loa/evals/ablation-2.0 plus a few edge vectors (1e21, 2**53+1 as float, strings with \u007f and  ) with both ablation-grade.sh's jcs and lib/jcs.sh and asserts equality.
findings.failure_scenario: When a future key manifest carries a numeric value above 2^53 (or a string with DEL/U+007F, which jq-based serialisers escape as \u007f and Python does not), then ablation-grade.sh and lib/jcs.sh compute different fixture_sha256 values for the same key and every verdict row is rejected as stale with a misleading 'the key changed' message.

findings.description: finding_ref derives the finding id from file and anchor_line only, while the reference (and so finding_sha256) also carries anchor_line_end when the citation is a range. credited_pairs keys on (id, defect) with setdefault, so two citations that share file:line but differ in end line (e.g. 'foo.py:10' and 'foo.py:10-20') yield one finding id whose finding_sha256 differs between the pairs each citation happens to credit first. The header states 'the same file and line are one finding', but the grade can list the same finding_id with two different finding_sha256 values across credited_pairs, and the stale check at 'r["finding_sha256"] != jcs_sha(pairs[key])' is per pair.
findings.failure_mode: When a judge tool derives one canonical reference per finding id (as the C-11 id derivation invites) rather than copying finding_sha256 per pair from credited_pairs, then its rows for the second pair are rejected as 'stale verdict - finding_sha256 is not F-xxxxxx's' although the finding and the key are unchanged, and the grade cannot be produced until the operator hand-edits the verdicts file.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the reference a function of the finding id alone: either drop anchor_line_end from the hashed reference, or include the end line in the id derivation input. Whichever is chosen, resolve the ref once per id (first citation wins, or widest range) and reuse it for every pair of that id so finding_sha256 is constant per finding_id in the listing.
findings.failure_scenario: When a judge tool derives one canonical reference per finding id (as the C-11 id derivation invites) rather than copying finding_sha256 per pair from credited_pairs, then its rows for the second pair are rejected as 'stale verdict - finding_sha256 is not F-xxxxxx's' although the finding and the key are unchanged, and the grade cannot be produced until the operator hand-edits the verdicts file.

findings.description: On reviewer concern 1: 'additive = no deleted lines' is not a sufficient mechanical proxy against weakening a floor gate written in bash. Purely added lines in verdict-derive.sh can neutralise existing checks: a second definition of a function later in the file replaces the first at call time; an inserted 'exit 0', 'return 0' or '[[ -n $X ]] && exit 0' ahead of the blocking tally short-circuits it; a re-assignment of a variable the scan reads (the severity regex, the trailer marker) after its original definition rewrites the rule; 'set +e'/'shopt' toggles or a 'trap ... EXIT' can rewrite the verdict after the check ran. None of these delete a line, so FS-1's additive test passes. The exact sha256 pin plus the DEC is the real control; the additive clause adds little assurance while the policy text presents it as a safeguard.
findings.failure_mode: When a cycle lands an amendment whose added lines include a late redefinition of the tally function or an early exit before the CRITICAL-bullet scan, then floor-snapshot FS-1 accepts the file at its pinned sha as 'additive', the gate reports APPROVED on a feedback file containing a CRITICAL bullet, and the floor mechanism provides no signal.
findings.suggested_fix: Strengthen FS-1 beyond line deletion: run verdict-derive.sh's own behavioural bats against the amended bytes as part of the floor test, and/or scan the added lines for a denylist of shape-changing tokens (function redefinition of an existing name, exit/return at top level, set +, trap, re-assignment of names defined in origin/main). Reword the floor.yaml comment so 'additive' is not presented as the safety property; the reviewed sha pin is.
findings.failure_scenario: When a cycle lands an amendment whose added lines include a late redefinition of the tally function or an early exit before the CRITICAL-bullet scan, then floor-snapshot FS-1 accepts the file at its pinned sha as 'additive', the gate reports APPROVED on a feedback file containing a CRITICAL bullet, and the floor mechanism provides no signal.
